newsitem.title: GEORGIA: Georgia blames Abkhazia, Russia for talks failure.
newsitem.headline: Georgia blames Abkhazia, Russia for talks failure.

text.p: Georgian officials blamed Abkhaz separatists and Russia on Sunday for the failure of U.N.- sponsored peace talks held in Geneva last week.

Foreign Minister Irakly Menagarishvili told reporters that three days of negotiations had made little headway in the vexing issue of resolving Abkhazia's status and the return of at least 150,000 ethnic Georgian refugees to the region.
Members of the Georgian negotiating team blamed Abkhaz officials and Russian mediators for trying to sabotage the talks from the start, the first held under U.N. auspices in some time.
Russia has mediated most negotiations between Georgia and the Black Sea province, which has been de facto independent since its irregulars drove out Georgian forces in 1993.

"The Russians and the Abkhaz were against the talks from the very start. All of the moves of the Abkhaz side were planned by the Russians," said Levan Aleksidze, foreign affairs adviser to President Eduard Shevardnadze.
"The Russians openly said that holding talks under the aegis of the United Nations is not in their interests," said Revaz Adamia, head of the Georgian parliament's security committee.
Aleksidze and Adamia said Russia resented U.N. involvement in resolving disputes in the former Soviet republics which Moscow still sees as its zone of influence.
"There was no point in continuing the talks at this stage," Adamia said, adding that they might resume in September.
Georgia offers Abkhazia strong autonomy within a federal state. Abkhazia says it will only agree to a union state in which it would be an equal member.
Tbilisi says that is just a smokescreen which would give Abkhazia the right to tear up the agreement at any time and declare full independence.

The talks also brought no progress on the return to Abkhazia of at least 150,000 ethnic Georgian refugees. Georgians once accounted for 45 percent of the region's population but are a small minority now in Abkhazia.
The only concrete agreement to come out of the talks was a pledge by the two sides that disputes would be settled "exclusively by political means".
Georgia has said it will not agree to the renewal of the mandate for 1,500 Russian peacekeepers patrolling a buffer zone between itself and Abkhazia unless changes in the forces' functions are made.
The mandate runs out at the end of the month, and Georgia has said the Russians must go if there is no accord on a new-style force.

Shevardnadze has said many Western leaders, worried that peacekeepers' withdrawals could lead to a new war, had urged him to let the Russians stay on. He has suggested in recent days that the mandate might be renewed.
